quote: Ob mit od. ohne Archimedes beweisbar S. 117 u. S. 130
english: Whether provable with or without Archimedes (the Archimedean axiom), p. 117 and p. 130.
topic: An index-like list of notes with page references to notebook III on the foundations of mathematics: proper functions, an axiom that every equation has a root, axiom layers as rings, provability with or without the Archimedean axiom, where mathematics begins, consistency as existence, and a defence against Frege.

triage.modern_statement: This is a cross-reference in an index, not a theorem stated in full. The question it points to is a standard one in Hilbert's axiomatic geometry: given the axioms of incidence, order, congruence and parallels, can a particular theorem be proved without the Archimedean axiom (Axiom V.1, the axiom of measure), or is that axiom needed? In modern terms, does the theorem hold in every model of the other axioms, including geometries built over non-Archimedean ordered fields? The notebook III entries on pp. 117 and 130 that would name the theorem(s) are not available, so the exact target cannot be identified. Known cases from this programme include Pascal's (Pappus's) theorem and the algebra of segments, the theory of proportion and area, and Legendre's angle-sum theorems.
triage.answered_by: Mostly Hilbert himself in Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899; 2nd ed. 1903). He proved Pascal's theorem and built segment arithmetic, proportion and area theory without the Archimedean axiom, and he studied non-Archimedean geometries and the commutative law of multiplication for non-Archimedean number systems. For Legendre's angle-sum theorems, Max Dehn answered it in his 1900 Göttingen dissertation 'Die Legendre'schen Sätze über die Winkelsumme im Dreieck'. Dehn showed that without the Archimedean axiom one Legendre theorem fails, using non-Legendrian and semi-Euclidean 'Dehn planes' over non-Archimedean fields. Hilbert cited these counterexamples.

evidence.claim: Dehn's dissertation, written under Hilbert, showed that Legendre's theorem that a triangle's angle sum is not greater than two right angles cannot be proved without the Archimedean postulate.
Dehn's dissertation is titled 'Die Legendre'schen Sätze über die Winkelsumme im Dreieck' (1900).

Hilbert's axiom system covers geometries over non-Archimedean fields. Hilbert (1900) cites Dehn's counterexamples to Legendre's theorem when the Archimedean axiom is dropped, and Dehn planes over non-Archimedean fields were used for independence proofs.
Dehn planes: non-Legendrian and semi-Euclidean geometries with infinitely many parallels through a point, but with angle sums of at least π.

The Foundations of Geometry has sections on non-Archimedean geometry, proofs of Pascal's theorem, segment algebra based on Pascal's theorem, the commutative law of multiplication for Archimedean and non-Archimedean number systems, and whether Pascal's theorem can be proved.
A contemporary review of Grundlagen der Geometrie notes that Pascal's proposition can be proved from axioms I, II, III and IV, without the Archimedean axiom.

triage.why: The note only says 'whether provable with or without Archimedes' and points to pages of another notebook, so the exact theorem cannot be pinned down. The theme, though, is clearly the role of the Archimedean axiom in Hilbert's foundations of geometry. That question was worked out in Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899/1903) and in Dehn's 1900 dissertation on Legendre's theorems. It is not one of the 23 problems and is classical, settled material. Confidence is only medium because the specific theorem(s) on pp. 117 and 130 of notebook III cannot be checked.
